name: Muroji Shoyu (Fukui, claimed oldest surviving shoyu house)
text: Shoyu brewery in Fukui city that gives its founding as 1573 (Tensho 1) and describes itself on its own site as the oldest existing shoyu maker in Japan after about 450 years in Echizen/Fukui. The 'oldest' claim is the company's and is repeated in a column; it should be treated as self-description, not independently verified. The house stresses natural (unforced, season-driven) brewing.
flavor: Natural-brew shoyu character; specific tasting notes not given in the sources seen.
use: Table and cooking shoyu from a long-running Fukui house; useful as a reference point for traditional Echizen-style natural-fermentation shoyu.
craft: Check what 'natural brewing' means in practice (no heated or accelerated fermentation, fermentation across the seasons) and ask the maker for the barrel type and aging time per grade; neither is stated in the search summaries.
src: Column on Japan's oldest shoyu house, Fukui

name: Komego (Fukui miso house, Eiheiji purveyor)
text: Miso house in Fukui city founded in Tenpo 2 (1831) and known as a purveyor to Eiheiji temple. It keeps making miso with kura-resident (house) yeast. It runs a miso theme-park facility, 'Miso-raku', where visitors can see the brewery and learn about fermented foods.
flavor: House-yeast fermented miso; flavour detail not given in the sources seen.
use: Miso for soups and cooking; the Eiheiji connection links it to temple (shojin) cooking in Fukui.
craft: Resident-yeast fermentation means each kura's flora is part of the product; when comparing lots, note season of brewing and aging length, which the source does not specify.

name: Yamasakiya (Tama Shoyu, Fukui)
ja: たま醤油 山さきや
text: Shoyu maker in Fukui city whose site gives its founding as Kyoho 2 (1717). Its product name 'Tama Shoyu' (玉醤油) is explained as a name granted by the domain lord. It is also listed among the members of the Fukui Prefecture Shoyu-Miso Industry Cooperative, which offers factory tours.
flavor: Not described in the sources seen.
use: Traditional Fukui table shoyu; useful when sourcing regional shoyu with documented Edo-period lineage.
craft: Founding year and the origin of the 'Tama' name are the maker's own account; confirm with the maker before citing in print. Production details (barrels, koji ratio) are not in the sources.
src: Fukui Shoyu-Miso Industry Cooperative: factory tours

name: Nomura Shoyu (Ono, Fukui)
text: Shoyu and miso brewery in Ono city, Fukui, said to date from the early Meiji period. The first-generation owner reportedly began brewing miso and shoyu by applying his barrel-making (cooperage) skills. It is described as a purveyor to Eiheiji. The listing appears on the Shoyu Information Center's brewery guide.
flavor: Not described in the sources seen.
use: Regional shoyu and miso of the Ono/Eiheiji area.
craft: The cooper origin story suggests a house built around wooden-barrel work; verify current barrel use and capacity with the maker.

name: Hamada Shoyu Miso Jozo (Matsuoka, Eiheiji)
text: Shoyu and miso brewery in the Matsuoka district of Eiheiji town, Fukui, founded in Taisho 14 (1925). It is known for natural fermentation in wooden barrels (kioke), staying with traditional equipment rather than steel tanks.
flavor: Wooden-barrel, naturally fermented shoyu and miso; detailed tasting notes not given in sources.
use: Cooking and table shoyu and miso for those who want kioke-brewed Fukui product.
craft: With kioke natural brewing, batch-to-batch and seasonal variation is expected; ask for the vintage and aging period of each lot.
src: Fukui Shoyu-Miso Industry Cooperative: factory tours

name: Masuichi Ichimura Shuzojo (Obuse)
text: Sake brewery in Obuse, Nagano, continuing since Horeki 5 (1755). A regional tourism guide singles it out for kioke (wooden-barrel) brewing and for traditional methods in which much labor is invested. It is one of the Nagano breweries presented to visitors in the Nagano/Obuse area.
flavor: Kioke-brewed sake; style details not given in sources.
use: Regional sake from a brewery with an Edo-period lineage in a town that is also known as a tourist destination.
craft: Kioke brewing implies wooden-vessel handling and hygiene discipline; ask which stages (fermentation, pressing, aging) are wooden.
src: Nagano sake brewery guide, Nagano City CVB

name: Nitta Jozo (Sakaki, Shinshu miso)
text: Miso maker in Sakaki town, Nagano, founded at the end of the Edo period and listed among visit-friendly Shinshu miso kura. It is described as making Shinshu miso in wooden barrels (kioke shikomi), the traditional method.
flavor: Wooden-barrel Shinshu miso, a rice-koji miso; no tasting detail in the sources.
use: Shinshu-type miso for soups, nuruka marinades and cooking; also an example of a kura open to visitors.
craft: For kioke miso, ask barrel age, fermentation period and whether it is sold unpasteurized, as enzymes and yeast stay active.
src: Go Nagano: Shinshu miso kura to visit

name: Maru-sho Jozo (Matsumoto, Shinshu miso and shoyu)
text: Shinshu miso and shoyu brewery in Matsumoto, Nagano, founded in Meiji 28 (1895) according to its own site. It is listed among the Shinshu miso kura to visit.
flavor: Shinshu miso and shoyu; no tasting detail in the sources.
use: Everyday Shinshu miso for soups and cooking, and shoyu from the same house.
craft: Details of process (koji ratio, barrel or tank) are not in the search summaries; ask the maker.
src: Go Nagano: Shinshu miso kura to visit

name: Suyakame (Nagano, monzen miso)
text: Miso maker near Zenko-ji temple in Nagano city, founded in the Meiji period and described as a 120-year-old business. It sells Shinshu miso and 'monzen miso' (the miso of the temple-gate district) at a direct shop and also runs a restaurant on site.
flavor: Shinshu / Zenko-ji monzen miso; no tasting detail in the sources.
use: Table miso and miso-based dishes tied to the Zenko-ji district.
craft: The Meiji founding and '120 years' are approximate, from the maker's and tourism pages.
src: Go Nagano: Shinshu miso kura to visit

name: Ishii Miso (Matsumoto)
text: Miso brewery in Matsumoto, Nagano, founded in 1868 and noted for brewing in cedar barrels in a traditional manner. It appears in the Nagano tourism guide to Shinshu miso kura.
flavor: Cedar-barrel Shinshu miso; no tasting detail in the sources.
use: Shinshu miso for soups and cooking; a kura example for the cedar-barrel method.
craft: Cedar barrels are porous and age with the miso; ask barrel age and rotation practice.
src: Go Nagano: Shinshu miso kura to visit

name: Yoro Shuzo (Sake Kura Kai, Yamanashi City)
text: Sake brewery in Yamanashi city, Yamanashi. The prefectural tourism site calls it the only brewery in Yamanashi city and the smallest in the prefecture. The brewery can be visited only on the annual kura-biraki open day, held on the second Sunday of February. A cafe-restaurant, 'Sake Kura Kai', operates on the premises. The founding year is not given in the results seen.
flavor: Small-batch local sake; no style detail in the sources.
use: Local sake for Yamanashi; the open day is the practical way for buyers and chefs to taste the full range.
craft: A very small brewery means limited lots; check availability directly with the kura.
src: Yamanashi prefecture tourism: Sake Kura Kai

name: Nakashima Jozo (Mizunami)
text: Sake brewery in Mizunami, Gifu, with a founding year of 1702 given in a Gifu sake column; this is the oldest of the examples listed there. Gifu's prefectural tourism site notes that many breweries in the prefecture are over 100 years old and that quality underground water and a cool climate support sake making. Further product details are not in the sources seen.
flavor: Not described in the sources seen.
use: Gifu junmai and regional sake; a reference house for Edo-period Mino brewing.
craft: Only the founding year is sourced; verify brand lineup, rice and yeast with the brewery.

name: Harada Shuzoba (Takayama)
text: Sake brewery in Takayama, Gifu, whose founding is given as 1855 in a Gifu sake column. Takayama is a mountain city where brewing is supported by the cold winter climate and clean water. Further product details are not in the sources seen.
flavor: Not described in the sources seen.
use: Hida/Takayama regional sake.
craft: Only founding year and town are sourced; ask the brewery about rice (Hida-grown or otherwise) and brewing season.

name: Miwa Shuzo (Ogaki)
text: Sake brewery in Ogaki, Gifu, founded in 1837 according to a Gifu sake column that lists it among the prefecture's breweries over 100 years old. Ogaki sits in the water-rich Mino plain. Product details are not in the sources seen.
flavor: Not described in the sources seen.
use: Mino regional sake.
craft: Only founding year and town are sourced.

name: Chikumeido (Shizuoka tea merchant)
text: Shizuoka city tea merchant founded in 1781 (Tenmei 1), specializing in retail sale of Shizuoka tea. It is regularly named among the city's long-established tea shops.
flavor: Shizuoka sencha-style teas; tasting notes not in the sources.
use: Retail tea source for Shizuoka sencha; a reference for buying blended and single-origin Shizuoka tea.
craft: As a retailer-blender its skill is in selection and blending (gokoh) from wholesale lots; ask for the harvest date and origin of each lot.
src: Tabirai: Shizuoka tea shops and cafes

name: Koyamaen Chaho (Shizuoka)
text: Shizuoka city tea shop founded in 1865, run as the direct-sale shop of a tea wholesaler-processor (seicha tonya). Shizuoka's seicha tonya buy raw tea from farmers, refine and blend it, then sell it on, which is the core trade this firm is built on. Not to be confused with the Uji-area matcha maker of a similar name.
flavor: Shizuoka blended teas; tasting notes not in the sources.
use: Direct purchase of finished Shizuoka teas from a wholesaler's own shop.
craft: Ask about the refining (shiage) and firing step, which is where a tonya's house style is set.
src: Tabirai: Shizuoka tea shops and cafes

name: Shirakata Denshiro Shoten (Shizuoka)
text: Shizuoka tea wholesaler-processor (seicha tonya) founded in Taisho 12 (1923). It is one of the long-established Shizuoka tea houses that refine and blend raw tea bought from producers.
flavor: Shizuoka tea; tasting notes not in the sources.
use: Shizuoka tea for retail and trade purchasing.
craft: Only the founding year and role are sourced.

name: Tamaruya Honten (Shizuoka wasabi-zuke)
text: Shizuoka wasabi-zuke maker, founded in Meiji 8 (1875) according to a Shizuoka tourism listing. It cultivates its own wasabi in the Abe-oku mountains, regarded as the birthplace of wasabi cultivation, and in Fujinomiya, and offers factory visits.
flavor: Wasabi pickled with sake lees; the pungent, sweet-savory style of Shizuoka wasabi-zuke.
use: Wasabi-zuke as a rice accompaniment or garnish; a chef sources it for its own-field wasabi.
craft: Ask which wasabi (stems, leaves) and what ratio of lees and salt are used; the sources do not state them.

name: Tamura Shokuhin (Numazu wasabi-zuke)
text: Wasabi-zuke maker in Numazu, Shizuoka, founded in 1925. According to Shizuoka tourism and its own site, it uses Izu wasabi and sake lees of ginjo grade or above.
flavor: Wasabi in ginjo sake lees; sweet-sharp.
use: Wasabi-zuke for rice, tea-over-rice or as a small plate with sake.
craft: Lees quality is the variable that sets sweetness and aroma; ginjo-or-above lees is the stated standard.

name: Nozakura Wasabi-zuke (Shizuoka)
text: Wasabi-zuke maker founded in Ansei 5 (1858), according to a Shizuoka tourism listing. It is described as pickling its wasabi with just sake lees and salt, a minimal two-ingredient preparation.
flavor: Pure wasabi and sake-lees flavor, without added sweeteners per the description.
use: Wasabi-zuke as a condiment and sake snack.
craft: A lees-and-salt-only cure leaves the wasabi's own heat prominent; check the salt level before using in seasoned dishes.

name: Yanagiya Honten (Yaizu katsuobushi)
text: Katsuobushi maker in Yaizu, Shizuoka, founded in the early Meiji era. It makes both arabushi (simmered, smoke-dried; roughly two weeks of production) and karebushi (mold-cured; roughly six months). A Shizuoka newspaper report on another Yaizu maker, Yamanana, which stopped making katsuobushi after 116 years, cites falling demand for honkarebushi and rising bonito prices; a Yaizu shopkeeper estimates over 90 percent of local product is now arabushi.
flavor: Arabushi is smoky and assertive; karebushi is mellower and cleaner.
use: Arabushi for strong, quick dashi and seasoning; karebushi for refined clear soups.
craft: The two product types differ in process length (about 2 weeks versus about 6 months with mold cultures); judge karebushi by clean mold aroma and dry, metallic ring when struck.
src: Shizuoka Shimbun: Yamanana exits katsuobushi production

name: Yamajuu (Yaizu tebiyama katsuobushi)
text: Yaizu katsuobushi workshop founded in Meiji 20 (1887), noted for the traditional tebiyama-zukuri method. The company runs a direct shop where freshly shaved katsuobushi is sold. Yaizu has the largest landings of frozen bonito in Japan, which underpins its katsuobushi trade.
flavor: Smoky, freshly shaved katsuobushi aroma.
use: Freshly shaved flakes for dashi, topping and finishing.
craft: Tebiyama is a hand-managed smoking method; the source gives no temperature or duration. Buy shaved to order, as aroma fades after shaving.

name: Kakukyu (Hatcho Miso, Okazaki)
ja: カクキュー(合資会社八丁味噌)
text: Okazaki hatcho miso maker, whose founding is given as Shoho 2 (1645), based on an 1878 petition by the Hayakawa family to the Aichi prefectural office. Tradition says the first generation, Hayakawa Kyuemon Katsuhisa, was a retainer of Imagawa Yoshimoto and learned miso making after leaving the samurai life after the Battle of Okehazama. Hatcho miso is a long-aged soybean (mame) miso, made now by only two firms in Okazaki. Kakukyu brews in wooden barrels topped with natural river stones from the upper Yahagi river, piled by hand in a cone as weights.
flavor: Dense, long-aged soybean miso; tasting notes not in sources.
use: Red miso soup, miso-nikomi, dengaku and stews, where long cooking suits it.
craft: The weights are hand-stacked stones; cone-shaped stacking keeps even pressure over a barrel. Founding year is a traditional claim rather than independently established.

name: Maruya Hatcho Miso (Okazaki)
text: Okazaki hatcho miso maker, which states a founding date of Enmoto 2 (1337) on its official site and began in brewing. It sits on the old Tokaido road, eight cho (about 870 m) west of Okazaki Castle, which gives hatcho miso its name. Along with Kakukyu it is one of the only two makers of the traditional product.
flavor: Dense, long-aged soybean miso; tasting notes not in sources.
use: Red miso soup, nikomi dishes, dengaku, and as a base for rich sauces.
craft: The 1337 date is the company's claim; the Okazaki tourism association repeats it, but founding dates differ between the two houses (Kakukyu 1645) and are not independently verified.
src: Colocal: the two hatcho miso kura

name: Kokonoe Mirin (Hekinan)
text: Mirin maker in Hekinan, Aichi, founded in 1772 and described as the oldest surviving hon-mirin specialist in Japan. Its flagship, Hon-mirin Kokonoe Sakura, is noted for an honorary grand prize at national liquor competitions from the Taisho to Showa periods (the only one given, per the source).
flavor: True mirin: sweetness from rice saccharification with mellow rice-wine aroma.
use: Hon-mirin for glazes, simmered dishes and sauces; also drinkable.
craft: Hon-mirin is made from glutinous rice, koji and shochu or spirit, saccharified over a long period; the sources cited here do not give the schedule.

name: Sugiura Mirin (Hekinan)
text: Hekinan, Aichi mirin maker founded in Taisho 13 (1924), known for old-style Mikawa shikomi (koshiki Mikawa shikomi) mirin. Hekinan and the surrounding Mikawa area are Japan's best-known mirin region.
flavor: Old-style mirin; sweetness and rice aroma, no further detail in sources.
use: Hon-mirin for cooking and glazes.
craft: The 'koshiki Mikawa' label refers to the old local brewing method; get the maker's own definition of the steps.

name: Tokai Jozo (Suzuka, Ise Kaido)
text: Brewery in Suzuka, Mie, founded in the Genroku era (1688-1704) and billed as the 300-year Ise Kaido kura. It makes miso and tamari, soy products rooted in the Tokai region's soybean-based seasonings.
flavor: Soy-based miso and tamari; no tasting detail in sources.
use: Miso and tamari for dengaku, sashimi dipping and cooking.
craft: Founding era is given loosely as 'Genroku'; a specific year is not in the sources.

name: Tomita Shuzo (Nagahama, Shichihonyari)
text: Sake brewery in Kinomoto, Nagahama, Shiga, founded in 1534 (Tenbun era). Its brand Shichihonyari is known as a sake loved by the artist Kitaoji Rosanjin. It is among Shiga's oldest breweries.
flavor: Sake of the northern Lake Biwa area; detailed profile not in sources.
use: Regional sake for northern Omi cuisine.
craft: The founding date is given by tourism features; the Rosanjin association is a well-known brand story, not a technical credential.

name: Uehara Shuzo (Shiga, wooden lever press)
text: Brewery on the northwest of Lake Biwa founded in Bunkyu 2 (1862). It is cited for using the mokuso tenbin shibori, a wooden-trough, lever-weight press that is now rare across Japan.
flavor: Sake pressed by lever and weight; flavor notes not in sources.
use: Regional sake of Takashima.
craft: The tenbin press uses a long beam and weight to apply slow, gentle pressure; ask about pressing duration and fraction cuts.
src: Biwako Visitors: sake kura in Shiga

name: Okamura Honke (Toyosato, Shiga)
text: Toyosato, Shiga brewery said to have started in 1854 on the order of the Hikone domain's chief elder, the Ii family. It still uses traditional wooden-trough pressing. Another article calls it a 160-year-old house, which is inconsistent with the 1854 date.
flavor: Wooden-trough pressed sake; no tasting detail in sources.
use: Shiga regional sake.
craft: Sources disagree on age; check with the brewery. Wooden pressing (kisou) is a slow and labor-intensive method.
src: Biwako Visitors: sake kura in Shiga

name: Ota Shuzo (Kusatsu)
text: Brewery in Kusatsu, Shiga, along an old highway, founded in 1874. The brewery traces its history to the Muromachi period, with an ancestor claimed to be the Muromachi warrior Ota Dokan.
flavor: Local sake of the old Tokaido post town.
use: Shiga regional sake.
craft: The Muromachi lineage is the maker's story; the 1874 date is the formal founding.

name: Gekkeikan (Fushimi)
text: Fushimi sake brewer founded in Kanei 14 (1637) by Okura Jiemon, who came from Kasagi to Fushimi. The early brand was 'Tama no Izumi'; the name Gekkeikan was adopted in 1905 (Meiji 38).
flavor: Not described in the sources seen.
use: Wide range of sake from table to premium grades.
craft: The sources give only founder, dates and brand history; ask the brewer for process details.

name: Kinshi Masamune (Fushimi)
text: Sake brewery founded in Tenmei 1 (1781) on Sakaimachi-dori in central Kyoto, using the area's good water, and moved to Fushimi in Meiji 13 (1880).
flavor: Fushimi-style sake; no detail in sources.
use: Sake for Kyoto cuisine.
craft: The move from the city center to Fushimi in 1880 reflects Fushimi's rise as the main sake district.
src: Fushimi Sake Brewers' Association: Kinshi Masamune

name: Yamamoto Honke (Shinsei, Fushimi)
text: Fushimi sake brewery founded in Enpo 5 (1677) at Aburakake, then the center of Fushimi. The first generation is recorded as Shioya Genbei; the house is also said to have made miso and shoyu at the start. Its brand is Shinsei.
flavor: Fushimi sake; no detail in sources.
use: Sake for Kyoto cuisine.
craft: The early miso and shoyu trade is noted with 'seems to' in the source; treat it as likely, not certain.
src: Fushimi Sake Brewers' Association: Yamamoto Honke

name: Matsumoto Shuzo (Sawaya, Fushimi)
text: Brewery founded in Kansei 3 (1791) by Matsumoto Jihei in what is now Higashiyama ward, Kyoto, under the trade name Sawaya, and moved to its present Fushimi site in Taisho 11 (1922).
flavor: Fushimi sake; no detail in sources.
use: Sake for Kyoto cuisine.
craft: Sawaya was the original name of the brand.

name: Ippodo Tea (Kyoto)
text: Kyoto tea merchant founded in Kyoho 2 (1717), originally as Omiya. The name 'Ippodo' was bestowed by the Yamashina no Miya imperial family. It is a specialist in Japanese tea with a main shop in Kyoto and a Tokyo Marunouchi branch.
flavor: Kyoto/Uji teas; not described in sources.
use: Matcha, gyokuro, sencha and hojicha for hospitality and cooking.
craft: Specialist tea retail; ask for harvest dates.

name: Senmaizuke Honke Daito (Kyoto)
text: Kyoto pickle shop that is recognized as the originator of senmaizuke (thinly sliced turnip pickle). The first generation, Daikokuya Totaro, had been a kitchen official of the Imperial Court's Daizenryo, and began selling pickles in Keio 1 (1865).
flavor: Thin turnip slices pickled with kombu; sweet-tangy, as senmaizuke is generally.
use: Winter table pickle and kaiseki accompaniment.
craft: The founding year of pickle trade is 1865, but the origin of the pickle's invention is the shop's own account.

name: Murakami-Juu Honten (Kyoto senmaizuke)
text: Kyoto pickle house famed for senmaizuke. One interview source gives its founding as Tenpo 3 (1832), while another article calls it 180 years old, so the dating differs by source. Senmaizuke is made from November to the end of February.
flavor: Sliced turnip pickle, sweet and gently sour.
use: Winter pickle plate and kaiseki.
craft: Production is seasonal, tied to the turnip harvest; source dates for the founding disagree.
